What helps and why it's different for each

sections.title: Is freeze the same as shutdown?
How do I know which state I'm in?

blocks.p: One is limp. One is tense. They're often confused. Telling them apart changes everything.
Here's the short version: shutdown is collapse. The body goes limp, heavy, numb, and drained of energy. Freeze is the opposite. The body tenses with an energetic charge underneath.
Shutdown and freeze are both your nervous system's ways of immobilizing you to help you survive. They feel completely different, and they need different things from you.

blocks.h3: Am I in shutdown or freeze?

blocks.p: The realistic but unclear answer is… both.

We all have some level of shutdown or freeze within us (and flight/fight and safety, too). Some events, seasons, people, or places are more likely to put us into freeze or shutdown. You've probably experienced periods of freeze during a panic attack or overwhelm. Stress is a mild version of freeze. And you've probably experienced shutdown when sad or grieving.
Of course, you're asking more specifically. "Yes, but which state am I in: freeze or shutdown?" Got it. Let's talk about what makes them what they are, and a third immobilization option.

blocks.h: Shutdown and freeze are both immobility

blocks.p: Freeze and shutdown are both your body's attempts to immobilize in the face of danger. They just have different flavors. Freeze is tense, and shutdown is collapsed. The body has a third flavor of immobilization as well: stillness. (Yes, that one is more pleasant. And yes, it's possible to get there.)

Why the different flavors of immobility? Well, you get different cake flavors from mixing different ingredients, right? Same with the body's immobilization. Here are the neurobiological ingredients to make an immobilization cake:

As these different biological pathways are active to different intensities, the body mobilizes or immobilizes. So, when the body is in a dominant dorsal state, it collapses in shutdown. When it's in a dominant dorsal and sympathetic, it tenses in freeze. And when the body has enough ventral and dorsal, then it relaxes into stillness.
Back to the question of, "Which state am I in?"

ol: Notice your body for a moment. Don't fix or control. It might help to take one intentional big breath and let it out slowly before noticing your body.
Limp, or stiff? Heavy and draining, sinking and slumped, or braced and rigid, jaw tight, shoulders up, locked? Is there tension in your immobility or not? Are you more collapsed or upright?
Gone, or energized? Far away, foggy, energy low, or surrounded by stimuli that you can't shake, engine running but can't move?

blocks.p: If you're identifying more of the heavy, numb, far away, and low-energy, that generally points toward shutdown. Tense, energized, overwhelmed points toward freeze.
A quick word on dissociation, because people often ask where it comes from.

Dissociation isn't a separate state on top of freeze or shutdown. It seems to be something the dorsal vagal state can produce at the extreme. Feeling far away, foggy, watching yourself from outside, disconnected from your body or your surroundings: that's the checked-out quality severe shutdown can bring with it. The further the body sinks, the more likely it is to come along.
And because shutdown is part of freeze (remember the ingredients: freeze is dorsal collapse with a sympathetic charge layer), dissociation can show up in freeze too.
Dissociation isn't a fourth immobilization box to sort yourself into. It's a potential experience of severe dorsal vagal activation.

blocks.h: What helps and why it's different for each

blocks.p: This isn't a vocabulary nitpick. The two states have different underlying mechanisms and need different things to regain mobility and regulation.

Shutdown has very little energy. The body has collapsed, and coming back is a slow, gentle re-warming: small movement, a little sensation, a quiet cue of safety. Pushing hard against shutdown tends to deepen it.

Freeze has the opposite problem: it contains a lot of charge, which is pinned by the immobilization. It isn't only about settling down, nor about forcing the energy out. It's about adding enough safety that the brake can lift. When a body genuinely senses it's safe, the immobilization eases, and the mobilization underneath it can finally resolve rather than staying clamped in place.

Freeze and shutdown both require the same thing to regulate out of stuckness, in essence: more safety. But you can't just choose to add more safety into the mix. You add safety through small enough doses for the system to take in and integrate.

They both need safety, but the difference is what's waiting on the other side once enough safety is in place. With shutdown, you're filling the body back up from an empty collapse. It becomes fuller, more energized. With freeze, you're freeing up the frozen energy, giving it the freedom to shift.

blocks.why: Both states need the same thing first: more safety, in doses small enough to take in. This practice adds some.

blocks.p: "Just calm down" doesn't work for freeze. It backfires. The state isn't calmable yet. There's too much trapped mobilization within, and not enough safety for the body to release the brake holding it in. Push harder, and the body will shut down.
"Just snap out of it" doesn't work for shutdown. It's impossible to snap out of an empty collapse when there is no energy in the system to turn to.
You can learn more in the [freeze hub](hub:freeze) and the [shutdown hub](hub:shutdown), including how to come out of each.

blocks.h: Mental health "disorders" and stuck freeze and shutdown

blocks.p: If by now this is sounding like depression or anxiety or panic or fear, you're not wrong. Deb Dana puts it this way:

q: Through the lens of the polyvagal theory, almost every diagnosis in the DSM is a dysregulated nervous system.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [on the Stuck Not Broken podcast](https://youtu.be/tUzCnBec-2A)

blocks.p: A dysregulated nervous system shows up as overactive defense, like shutdown and freeze. The nervous system level of dysregulation manifests as uncomfortable internal sensations, conscious emotions, and thinking patterns.
Shutdown most commonly shows up as a major depressive disorder or dysthymia diagnosis. Thoughts become more pessimistic, and motivation wanes.

Freeze can show up many different ways, like panic disorder, phobias, intermittent explosive disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, and bipolar disorder. Thoughts become more catastrophic and overwhelming as fear and emotional intensity increase.

To cope with dysregulation, one will adopt various coping strategies to self-soothe. (These are called "behavioral adaptations.") In shutdown, one will increase isolation, reduce activities that require energy, and oversleep. To cope with dysregulated freeze, one may attempt to self-soothe through compulsions, binging, and relationship dependence.

blocks.h3: Is freeze the same as shutdown?

blocks.p: No. Shutdown is the body collapsing and going limp. Freeze is the body stiffening while it's still highly charged, combining sympathetic fight-or-flight energy with immobilization.
Yep. In panic, you're highly activated and fearful, but stuck in place, unable to move. High charge plus immobilization is the signature of freeze.

blocks.h3: How do I know which state I'm in?

blocks.p: Read the ingredients. Limp, heavy, numb, and far away leans toward shutdown. Stiff, charged, alert, and unable to move leans toward freeze. The quick exercise above walks you through it.
Because they ask for different things on the other side of safety. Knowing what state you're in will help you plan out adding safety and what to expect as regulation unfolds.
